Straw
STRAW
noun
From the Anglo-Saxon streaw, that which is strewn; rendering the Hebrew teben, the chopped stalks of grain left after threshing — used as fodder for cattle and as the binding temper mixed into mud brick.

Biblical Definition

Straw is the chopped stalk left when the grain is threshed out: worthless as food for men, indispensable as fodder for beasts and as the binder that holds a mud brick together. Its great appearance in Scripture is in Pharaoh’s answer to the word of the LORD. When Moses said, Let my people go, Pharaoh charged the taskmasters, “Thus saith Pharaoh, I will not give you straw” (Exo 5:10), and the quota stood unaltered: “Go therefore now, and work; for there shall no straw be given you, yet shall ye deliver the tale of bricks” (Exo 5:18). So Israel “was scattered abroad throughout all the land of Egypt to gather stubble instead of straw” (Exo 5:12) — the labour doubled, the standard unchanged, the officers beaten for the shortfall. It is one of the plainest pictures of tyranny in Scripture, and also one of the plainest of the law under a fallen man’s hand: a demand held at full height while the means of meeting it are taken away. Against that stands the picture at the other end of the Bible, where straw appears in the peace of the restored creation: “the lion shall eat straw like the ox” (Isa 11:7). The same humble fodder that measured Egypt’s cruelty measures the kingdom’s gentleness, when nothing in all God’s holy mountain shall hurt nor destroy.

Webster 1828 Definition

The stalk of grain left after threshing, used for fodder and as the binding temper in mud brick; withheld by Pharaoh while the quota of bricks stood unchanged.

expand to see more

STRAW, the stalk or stem of certain species of grain, pulse and grasses, particularly of wheat, rye, oats, barley and buckwheat.

From the Saxon streaw; that which is strewed or scattered.

It is used chiefly as fodder and litter for cattle, and formerly as a temper in unburnt brick.

In Scripture, Pharaoh withheld straw from the Israelites while requiring the same tale of bricks (Exo 5:7-18).

Proverbially, a thing of small value; but in Isaiah, the food of the lion in the peaceable kingdom (Isa 11:7).

Key Scripture

Exo 5:10 — "And the taskmasters of the people went out, and their officers, and they spake to the people, saying, Thus saith Pharaoh, I will not give you straw."

Exo 5:12 — "So the people were scattered abroad throughout all the land of Egypt to gather stubble instead of straw."

Exo 5:18 — "Go therefore now, and work; for there shall no straw be given you, yet shall ye deliver the tale of bricks."

Isa 11:7 — "And the cow and the bear shall feed; their young ones shall lie down together: and the lion shall eat straw like the ox."

Modern Corruption

“Bricks without straw” has been worn down into a workplace cliché for being under-resourced, emptied of the cruelty it named and of the deliverance that answered it.

expand to see more

The phrase survives in ordinary speech long after its meaning has been rubbed off. Men say they are being asked to make bricks without straw when a budget is cut or a deadline is short, and the comparison is not simply false — the pattern really is the same, a demand held at full height while the means are withdrawn — but it has been made trivial. In Exodus the officers of the children of Israel were beaten daily for the shortfall; the scattering over all the land to gather stubble was added to a day’s work already brutal; and the whole device was the deliberate retaliation of a king against the word of God. It was calculated cruelty with a theological aim: Pharaoh said, Ye are idle, ye are idle, therefore ye say, Let us go and do sacrifice to the LORD — treating the desire to worship as the sloth that justified the crackdown. That is how the world has always answered a people asking leave to serve God, and it deserves a stronger word than inconvenience.

Recover what the straw teaches about law and grace. Pharaoh is the picture of a taskmaster who raises the standard and withdraws the help, and it is precisely how sin and a guilty conscience deal with a man: the demand of righteousness stands at full height, and the sinner has no means whatever of meeting it. The law given by Moses does not lower the tale of bricks by one. But God does what Pharaoh never would — He supplies in His Son everything His own law requires, so that the righteousness of the law is fulfilled in us who walk not after the flesh but after the Spirit. Note also how the episode ends. The people, made worse off by the promise of deliverance, turned on Moses; Moses turned to the LORD and said, why is it that thou hast sent me? And the answer was not an explanation but a covenant name: I am the LORD, and I will bring you out from under the burdens of the Egyptians. Deliverance was never in doubt; only the timing was hidden.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew teben, chopped threshed stalk used for fodder and brick-temper, distinguished from qash, the stubble left standing in the field which Israel was driven to gather in its place.

expand to see more

Hebrew — teben (תבן), straw or chaff-stalk, chopped for cattle fodder and mixed as temper into mud brick.

Hebrew — qash (קש), stubble, the field-remnant Israel gathered when the straw was withheld (Exo 5:12); elsewhere a figure of what the fire consumes.

Hebrew — matkoneth (מתכנת), the measure or tale of bricks, the fixed quota held unchanged in Exo 5:8.

Saxon — streaw, that which is strewn or scattered; the same root gives English strew.

Use — without the binding straw a sun-dried brick crumbles; the withholding was a technical impossibility, not merely a hardship.

Usage

"“Thus saith Pharaoh, I will not give you straw — and yet ye shall deliver the tale of bricks.”"

"“They gathered stubble instead of straw, and were beaten for the difference.”"

"“The law never lowers the quota; grace supplies in Christ what the law demands.”"
